readerTitle: How Ryanair makes money selling seats for a few euros
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Ryanair) + 가상 계산 (항공편 손익분기) + 가상 적용 (사내 교육팀, 지역 도매 배송)
insight: 고정비가 큰 사업에서 이익은 가격보다 채운 비율로 결정된다. 손익분기선을 낮추고 그 위를 채우는 것이 핵심이다.
misconception: 싼 가격은 곧 낮은 이익이다. 가격을 낮추면 남는 돈도 줄어든다.

sources.text: Ryanair Holdings plc, Annual Reports (fleet, load factor, ancillary revenue, FY2021 results)
Ryanair quarterly results statements ("load factor active, yield passive" pricing policy)
Creaton, S. (2004). Ryanair: How a Small Irish Airline Conquered Europe. (early-1990s turnaround, Southwest visit)
항공편 손익분기 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "몇 유로짜리 좌석"은 Ryanair의 프로모션 요금으로 널리 보도된 내용이나, 게시 전 최근 사례로 다시 확인하세요. "팬데믹 전 대부분의 해에 유럽에서 가장 수익성 높은 항공사 중 하나"라는 표현도 연차보고서 기준으로 확인 필요.
1990년대 초 위기와 Michael O'Leary의 Southwest 방문 후 저비용 모델로 전환한 이야기는 Creaton(2004) 등에 나옵니다. 정확한 연도는 자료마다 조금 다르므로 카드에는 "early 1990s"로만 적었습니다.
"load factor active, yield passive"는 Ryanair 실적 발표에 반복 등장하는 표현입니다. 원문 문구를 게시 전 확인하세요.
탑승률이 보통 90% 이상이라는 내용과 부가수익이 매출의 큰 비중이라는 내용은 최근 연차보고서로 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체 비율을 쓰지 않았습니다.
FY2021(2021년 3월 결산)에 대규모 연간 손실을 보고했다는 내용은 연차보고서로 확인 필요. 카드에는 금액 없이 "a large annual loss"로만 적었습니다.
가상 계산: 189석 기준. 항공편 고정비 €7,500, 승객당 수입(운임+부가) €60, 승객당 비용 €10 → 승객당 €50 남음. 손익분기 7,500 ÷ 50 = 150명 = 150 ÷ 189 ≈ 79%. 만석 시 나머지 39명 × €50 = €1,950 이익. 189석은 Ryanair 737-800 좌석 배치로 알려진 숫자이나 확인 필요.

cards.title: How Ryanair makes money selling seats for a few euros
body: Ryanair, the Irish airline, is famous for promotional fares that cost less than a taxi to the airport.
Yet in most years before the pandemic, it was one of the most profitable airlines in Europe. The trick isn't in the price. It's in how full the plane is.

image.label: A full plane cabin with a tiny price tag on one seat
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 비행기 객실 단면, 좌석이 거의 다 찬 모습. 한 좌석에 아주 작은 가격표 "€5". 실제 항공사 로고와 도장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A week to go, and seats are empty.
body: You set prices for a low-fare airline. A flight leaves in seven days. Many seats are still unsold, and bookings are slow.
Once the plane takes off, an empty seat earns nothing forever. What do you do?

options.text: Raise the fare. Late bookers usually pay more
options.feedback: This works on busy routes with eager late travelers. On a slow flight, you protect the price but may fly with seats that earn nothing.
It avoids training customers to expect deals. But if demand doesn't come, the plane leaves with empty seats and the same costs.

options.text: Cut the fare until the plane fills
options.feedback: This is Ryanair's stated approach. You give up some price per seat to win passengers who each bring money in. The next cards show why that pays.

cards.title: Fill the plane first. Let the price follow.
body: In the early 1990s, Ryanair was struggling. Its leaders studied Southwest Airlines in the US and rebuilt the business around low costs.

Ryanair's results statements describe its pricing as **"load factor active, yield passive."** Load factor is the share of seats filled. Yield is the average fare. In plain words: fill the seats, even if it means lower fares.
It typically reports flying with planes more than 90% full.

cards.title: The break-even line
body: Once a flight is scheduled, most of its costs are fixed: the plane, the crew, most of the fuel. They barely change whether 100 or 189 people board.
So every flight has a **break-even point**: the number of passengers needed to cover its costs. Below that line, the flight loses money. Above it, nearly every extra passenger is profit.

image.label: Plane seats with a break-even line across the cabin
image.brief: 위에서 본 비행기 좌석 배치도. 앞쪽 좌석은 회색("Covers costs"), 가로 점선 "Break-even" 뒤쪽 좌석은 초록색("Profit"). 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: Software works the same way: servers and staff cost roughly the same whether 900 or 1,000 customers pay. Past break-even, each new paying user is mostly profit.

cards.title: One flight, 189 seats.
body: Each passenger leaves €50 toward the flight's costs. Break-even: €7,500 ÷ €50 = **150 passengers**, about 79% full. The last 39 seats bring €1,950. Nearly all the profit sits in the last fifth of the plane.

breakdown.label: Flight costs
breakdown.detail: Plane, crew, fuel. Same if the plane is half empty

breakdown.label: Per passenger out
breakdown.detail: Costs that come with each passenger

cards.title: Two ways to beat the line.
body: Ryanair worked on both sides. It **pushed break-even down** with low costs: one aircraft family, cheaper secondary airports, quick turnarounds and online booking.
It also raised what each passenger brings in. Fees for bags, priority boarding and seat choice make up a large share of its revenue. So a cheap fare can still clear the line.

cards.title: Any fixed slot works this way.
body: A company's in-house training team books a trainer and a room for a 30-seat workshop. Only 12 people sign up.

The cost is the same with 30. Inviting another department or partner staff, even at a small charge, adds value without adding cost. The team's question isn't "what does a seat cost?" but "how do we fill the room?"

cards.title: High fixed costs cut both ways.
body: When passengers vanish, the costs stay. During the pandemic, flights were grounded and Ryanair reported a large annual loss.
Cheap prices also only work if each sale still covers its own costs, and if extras don't drive customers away. Ryanair's fees have long drawn complaints. Filling seats is a lever, not a free pass.

cards.title: Now it's a delivery route.
body: You run a regional wholesaler. A daily truck route costs the same each day: driver, truck, fuel. The truck usually leaves about 60% full, and the route barely breaks even.
What's the smartest next move?

options.text: Offer new shops on that route a lower rate, plus paid extras like timed delivery
options.feedback: You fill space that already costs you money, and extras lift revenue per stop. Keep the low rate for spare space so it doesn't replace full-price orders.

options.text: Cut prices 20% for every customer to win more volume
options.feedback: It may fill the truck, but every existing order now brings in less. You'd need a lot more volume just to stand still.

options.text: Add a second truck to grow faster
options.feedback: It doubles the fixed costs before the first truck is full. Now you have two routes near the break-even line.

cards.title: When costs are fixed, profit lives in the last seats.
body: Find your break-even line, push it down with lower costs, then fill everything above it.
**Try it today:** pick one fixed slot in your business: a shift, a room, a truck, a class. How full must it be to cover its costs? How full is it now?
